# The Levy-Lieb Constrained-Search Formulation and Its Equivalence to Conditional Probability Minimization

## Introduction

The Levy-Lieb constrained-search formulation provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for density functional theory by formally defining the exact Hohenberg-Kohn functional for any N-representable electron density. This approach circumvents the limitations of the original Hohenberg-Kohn theorem, which relied on the existence of an external potential, by instead constructing the universal functional through a direct search over all antisymmetric wavefunctions that yield a given density. As a result, the constrained-search method offers a well-defined and general prescription for the energy functional that lies at the heart of modern electronic structure theory.

## Equivalence to Conditional Probability Minimization

A central result of this work is the demonstration that the Levy-Lieb formulation is mathematically equivalent to minimizing the correlation functional with respect to the N-1 conditional probability density. Rather than searching over the full space of wavefunctions constrained to reproduce a target density, the problem can be reformulated in terms of the conditional probability distribution that describes the arrangement of the remaining electrons given the position of a reference electron. This reformulation shifts the focus from the many-body wavefunction to a more physically transparent quantity, thereby providing an alternative but equally valid route to the exact functional.

In this equivalence, the variable N represents the number of electrons in the system. The conditional probability density is therefore defined over the coordinates of N-1 electrons, capturing the correlated behavior of the electronic ensemble once one particle's position has been fixed. This interpretation makes explicit the connection between the total electron count and the dimensionality of the conditional probability space over which the minimization is performed.

## Consequences and Implications

The consequences and implications of this equivalence merit careful analysis. By recasting the constrained search as a minimization over conditional probability densities, the formulation offers new conceptual insight into the structure of the exact functional and the role of electron correlation. This perspective may suggest alternative strategies for constructing approximations, as it links the correlation functional directly to a well-defined probabilistic object. Moreover, the equivalence clarifies the interplay between the electron density and the correlated motion of the remaining particles, deepening our theoretical understanding of the many-electron problem.

## Illustrative Example

To support and clarify these theoretical findings, a practical example is presented. This concrete application serves to illustrate how the abstract equivalence manifests in a specific case, making the formal results more accessible and demonstrating their validity. By working through a tangible system, the example reinforces the general arguments and provides a clear demonstration of how the conditional probability formulation reproduces the expected behavior of the exact functional.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results establish a meaningful connection between the Levy-Lieb constrained-search formulation and the minimization of the correlation functional over the N-1 conditional probability density. This equivalence not only enriches the theoretical framework of density functional theory but also opens potential avenues for developing new approximations grounded in a probabilistic understanding of electron correlation.

# Reformulating the Levy–Lieb Functional in Terms of the Conditional Probability Density

## Background and Motivation

Density functional theory rests on the Hohenberg–Kohn theorems, which establish that the ground-state properties of a many-electron system are determined uniquely by the one-electron density $\rho(\mathbf{r})$. Central to this framework is the universal functional $F[\rho]$, which encapsulates the kinetic energy and the electron–electron interaction independently of any external potential. While its existence is guaranteed, the original Hohenberg–Kohn construction offers no prescription for evaluating $F[\rho]$, and its domain is restricted to densities arising from ground-state wavefunctions (so-called *v*-representable densities).

The constrained-search formulation introduced by Levy and later refined by Lieb resolves both difficulties. It provides an explicit variational definition,

$$
F[\rho] \;=\; \min_{\Psi \to \rho}\; \big\langle \Psi \,\big|\, \hat{T} + \hat{V}_{ee} \,\big|\, \Psi \big\rangle,
$$

where the minimization runs over all antisymmetric $N$-electron wavefunctions $\Psi$ that reproduce the prescribed density $\rho(\mathbf{r})$. This construction extends the functional to the broader class of $N$-representable densities—those obtainable from *any* well-behaved antisymmetric wavefunction—and thereby places the exact functional on a rigorous and universally applicable footing.

## The Equivalence with the Conditional Probability Density

The present work demonstrates that this constrained search admits an exact and physically transparent reformulation. The key observation is that the squared modulus of the wavefunction, interpreted as the joint probability density of the $N$ electrons, can be factored as

$$
|\Psi(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{r}_N)|^2 \;=\; \frac{\rho(\mathbf{r}_1)}{N}\, f(\mathbf{r}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{r}_N \,|\, \mathbf{r}_1),
$$

where $f$ is the **conditional probability density** describing the arrangement of the remaining $N-1$ electrons given the position of one reference electron. Once the one-electron density $\rho$ is fixed by the constraint, all the residual variational freedom of $\Psi$—the freedom that governs electron correlation—resides entirely in this conditional density.

Consequently, the Levy–Lieb minimization over wavefunctions yielding a given $\rho$ can be recast, without approximation, as a minimization of the correlation functional with respect to the $N-1$ conditional probability density. The density itself plays the role of a fixed weighting factor, while the conditional distribution carries the burden of minimizing the interaction and kinetic contributions that define correlation. This shift in perspective isolates the genuinely difficult part of the problem—the many-body correlations—from the comparatively simple constraint of fixing $\rho$.

## Analysis Through a Practical Example

To make the consequences of this equivalence concrete, we examine a representative model system in which both the constrained search and the conditional-density minimization can be carried out and compared explicitly. Working through this example clarifies several points that remain obscure in the abstract formulation:

- **Locality of the optimization.** Because the conditional density is normalized for each position of the reference electron, the minimization acquires a natural pointwise structure, revealing how correlation adjusts locally in response to the fixed density.

- **Separation of roles.** The example illustrates how the one-electron density and the conditional distribution contribute distinctly to the total energy, disentangling the "geometric" information encoded in $\rho$ from the "correlational" information encoded in $f$.

- **Behavior of the correlation functional.** By tracking the optimal conditional density, one can observe directly how electron correlation reorganizes as parameters of the model are varied, providing intuition that is difficult to extract from the wavefunction picture alone.

## Implications and New Insight

Beyond its formal appeal, this equivalence sheds light on the intrinsic mathematical structure of the exact density functional. It shows that the exact $F[\rho]$ is, at its core, a statement about optimal conditional distributions, suggesting that approximations targeting the conditional probability density directly may offer a more natural and systematically improvable route than those framed in terms of the wavefunction or reduced density matrices. The reformulation also connects the constrained-search apparatus to concepts familiar from conditional-probability and information-theoretic descriptions of correlation, opening potential avenues for new functional approximations.

In summary, by identifying the constrained search with a minimization over the conditional probability density, this analysis offers both a clarified understanding of what the exact functional encodes and a fresh vantage point from which to pursue its practical construction.

## The Levy-Lieb Functional

The **Levy-Lieb functional** is a fundamental concept in Density Functional Theory (DFT), a cornerstone of quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics used to study the electronic structure of many-body systems.

### Background

Density Functional Theory, pioneered by Hohenberg and Kohn in 1964, established that the ground-state properties of a many-electron system can be determined solely from its electron density, rather than requiring the full many-body wavefunction. However, the original Hohenberg-Kohn theorems were formulated for densities arising from ground-state wavefunctions, which posed certain mathematical limitations.

### The Constrained-Search Formulation

In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Mel Levy and Elliott Lieb independently developed a more rigorous foundation through what is now called the **constrained-search formulation**. The Levy-Lieb functional is defined as:

$$F_{LL}[\rho] = \min_{\Psi \to \rho} \langle \Psi | \hat{T} + \hat{V}_{ee} | \Psi \rangle$$

Here, the minimization is performed over all antisymmetric wavefunctions Ψ that yield a given electron density ρ, where:
- **T̂** represents the kinetic energy operator
- **V̂ₑₑ** represents the electron-electron interaction

### Significance

This formulation offers several advantages:

1. **Universality**: The functional depends only on the density, independent of the external potential.
2. **Rigor**: It extends DFT to any *N*-representable density, resolving the *v*-representability problem.
3. **Foundation**: It provides a mathematically sound basis for the exact ground-state energy through variational minimization.

Lieb later refined this using tools from convex analysis, introducing the closely related **Lieb functional** based on Legendre transforms.

**Abstract**

The Levy–Lieb constrained-search formulation provides a rigorous, wavefunction-based definition of the universal density functional that underlies Hohenberg–Kohn density-functional theory, expressing the internal energy as an infimum of the kinetic-plus-interaction expectation value over all antisymmetric $N$-body states yielding a prescribed one-particle density $\rho$. In this work we recast this variational principle in terms of the conditional probability density that specifies the distribution of the remaining $N-1$ particles given the position of one, and we establish that the constrained search is exactly equivalent to the minimization of a correlation functional over the manifold of admissible conditional densities. Starting from the marginal and normalization constraints imposed by a fixed single-particle density, we show that the electron–electron interaction and internal kinetic contributions can be organized into a functional whose stationary points characterize the Levy–Lieb minimizer, and we prove that the two optimization problems share the same infimum and the same set of minimizing states. This reformulation clarifies the role of exchange and correlation as intrinsically encoded in the geometry of conditional distributions, offers a transparent decomposition of the universal functional into single-particle and correlation pieces, and yields explicit lower and upper bounds through simple trial conditional densities. We discuss the implications for the construction of approximate functionals, the derivation of exact conditions on the correlation energy, and connections to strictly-correlated-electron and optimal-transport formulations of the strong-coupling limit. The equivalence provides a unifying variational viewpoint that bridges the wavefunction and density-matrix descriptions of many-electron systems.

# Abstract

The Levy-Lieb constrained-search formulation of density functional theory defines the universal functional through minimization over all antisymmetric wavefunctions yielding a prescribed one-particle density. While formally exact, this high-dimensional minimization is computationally intractable and obscures the role of electron correlation. Here we present a reformulation of the Levy-Lieb functional in terms of a constrained minimization over correlation functionals defined on the space of N-representable densities. By decomposing the universal functional into a mean-field (Hartree) contribution and a residual correlation functional, we recast the search over wavefunctions as an optimization over admissible pair correlation structures consistent with a given density. We establish that the resulting correlation functional inherits the essential convexity and lower-semicontinuity properties required for a well-posed variational problem, and we characterize the conditions under which the infimum is attained. The N-representability constraints on the density are shown to translate into natural admissibility conditions on the correlation functional, providing a transparent separation between kinematic constraints and dynamical correlation effects. This perspective clarifies the mathematical structure of the exchange-correlation problem and suggests systematic approximation schemes based on hierarchies of correlation functionals. We discuss implications for the construction of approximate functionals and for the numerical treatment of strongly correlated systems, where conventional mean-field approaches fail.

---

*Keywords:* density functional theory, Levy-Lieb functional, constrained search, N-representability, electron correlation, convex analysis

**Result (Equivalence of the Levy–Lieb Functional and Conditional-Probability Minimization).** Let $\rho \in \mathcal{J}_N$ denote an admissible $N$-electron single-particle density, i.e. $\rho \geq 0$, $\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\rho\,dx = N$, and $\sqrt{\rho}\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$, and let the Levy–Lieb universal functional be defined by the constrained search
$$
F_{\mathrm{LL}}[\rho] \;=\; \inf_{\Psi \mapsto \rho}\; \big\langle \Psi,\, (\hat T + \hat V_{ee})\,\Psi \big\rangle,
$$
where the infimum is taken over normalized antisymmetric wavefunctions $\Psi \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^{3N})$ whose single-particle density equals $\rho$, and $\hat T$, $\hat V_{ee}$ are the kinetic-energy and electron–electron interaction operators, respectively. Writing the joint $N$-point probability density $|\Psi|^2$ in factored form as $|\Psi(x_1,\dots,x_N)|^2 = \tfrac{1}{N}\rho(x_1)\,P(x_2,\dots,x_N \mid x_1)$, so that $P(\,\cdot \mid x_1)$ is the conditional probability distribution of the remaining $N-1$ particles given one particle fixed at $x_1$, one may then define a correlation functional $\mathcal{C}[\rho; P]$ obtained by re-expressing $F_{\mathrm{LL}}$ entirely through $\rho$ and the family of conditional densities $P$. The result asserts that the constrained search is *equivalent* to the variational problem over conditional probabilities,
$$
F_{\mathrm{LL}}[\rho] \;=\; \min_{P \in \mathcal{P}_\rho} \; \mathcal{C}[\rho; P],
$$
where $\mathcal{P}_\rho$ denotes the set of admissible conditional distributions consistent with the marginal $\rho$ and with the fermionic (antisymmetry, positivity, and normalization) constraints, and the minimizer $P^\star$ recovers the conditional structure of the optimal $\Psi$; the two formulations therefore yield identical values of the universal functional and identical minimizing correlations, establishing that minimizing the correlation functional with respect to conditional probabilities is a faithful reformulation of the Levy–Lieb constrained-search principle.
